item.title: Constructivism
item.description:
Constructivism, alongside Realism and Liberalism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it believes states behave rationally within a anarchic system.Constructivism traditionally believes that states act not only on power in a material sense, but also based on shared values, ideas, and identities. State interest is shaped by identity, identity is shaped by historical, social, and political contexts which are sometimes shared between states. The common norms and values within a state manifest themselves in the acts of the state. It differs from realism and liberalism, which both take state interests as a given. But constructivism asks how these interests are formed and what influences them.Wendt, 1992 "Anarchy is what states make of it" Constructivism disagrees with both realism and liberalism. Anarchy guarantees neither conflict nor cooperation. Instead, anarchy leaves the power in the hands of states to guide how they interact.
Lecture 2 slides 14-16

item.title: Liberalism
item.description:
Liberalism, alongside Realism and Constructivism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it believes states behave rationally within a anarchic system.
Liberalism traditionally believes that conflict is not an inevitable consequence of the international system. Liberalism agrees with realism that the international system exists in anarchy. But liberalism differs in their belief that through mutually agreed upon rules, laws, organizations, and norms conflict can be avoided. Like Neoclassical realism, liberalism believes that the domestic politics of a state influence that states foreign policy. Ultimately liberalism recognizes that the institutions and norms have not yet prevented conflict entirely, but liberalism is underlined by the belief that international politics can become more stable and cooperative with the appropriate steps. Interdependence liberalism argues that economic exchange makes states dependent on one another. This consequently would make a conflict with that other state more expensive and disruptive. Thus the belief is that a rational state would be less likely to engage in that conflict, and would seek an alternative solution to resolve whatever issue there may be. A key example of this turned into a policy is the European Union and its predecessors.Republican liberalism argues that i a democratic system, domestic institutions constrain leaders. This argument is centered around the idea that leaders who hold power at the will of the electorate, will not want to fight a war which makes them unpopular, and therefore less likely to reelected. The idea for international relations is therefore that democratic countries will find alternative mechanisms through which to resolve disputes. Neoliberal institutionalism argues that global institutions facilitate cooperation even inside of an anarchic systems. For this theory, institutions can correct for the uncertainty that is a key assumption of realism. With reduced uncertainty states act with more trust for one another because the institutions provide a certain guarantee that other states will behave "appropriately".
Lecture 2 slides 10-13

item.title: Realism
item.description:
Realism, alongside Liberalism and Constructivism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it is concerned with power; which states have it, which do not, and how that influences state relations.Realism traditionally assumes that global politics is at its heart about power struggles between states. It believes this to be the case because for realists, the international system is one of anarchy. They argue that anarchy is the reality of the international system because there is no higher authority than the state. Consequently, states are said to first and foremost value survival and security as well as the pursuit of greater power. This is also called Power Politics. Though it is important to note that there is variation amongst realists and not all realist theories are the same.Classical realism sees power politics as a consequence of human nature. Classical realists argue that there is egoistic and selfish tendency to human nature which then manifests itself in state behavior. Morgenthau, 1962 "The social world is but a projection of human nature onto the collective plane" Neorealism, also called structural realism, argues that state behavior is first and foremost influenced by the (anarchic) structure of the international system. Unlike classical realism, human nature is not the cause of conflict. Instead they argue the anarchy of the international system is what causes competition. There are varying perspectives on how states react to structural pressures. Uncertainty The uncertainty described in neorealism comes from the fact that, in anarchy, there is no way to know for certain that another state is being honest. They may tell you they want to be friendly and maintain good relations, whilst at the same time mobilizing to invade you. This is then said to lead states to assume the worst, making them pursue power as a matter of security and self preservation in the event of conflict. The fundamental assumption of offensive neorealism is that, in an anarchic system, it is uncertainty of other states' intentions that push states to pursue more power for themselves. As such great powers pursue the greatest relative power possible. Offensive realists argue that great powers can only truly achieve regional hegemony as the greatest extent of their power.Defensive realism conceptualizes states as pursuing security, not power. The argument is that excessive power accumulation makes other states perceive you as a threat. If you expand too much (territorially or otherwise) other states will seek to counter-balance this strength which would have the consequence of reducing security. Instead of pursuing power for power's sake, states pursue security by utilizing "balancing strategies". There is internal balancing, which builds capabilities: arms manufacturing, infrastructure development suited for military use, or more direct security facilities like fortifications and air defenses). There is external balancing in the form of building alliances with other states. Finally states practice restraint which keeps them from being subject to counter-balancing.Neoclassical realism agrees with neorealism that anarchy matters, but they add another force: domestic factors. Domestic factors may include metrics like a state's capacity to act, the domestic politics and ruling ideology, leadership perceptions and decision-making. For neoclassical realists the dynamic works so that structural pressures provide boundaries on decision making whilst domestic factors shape the ultimate choice of the state.Example: Nazi Germany The Nazis did not expand due only to systemic pressure, but also due to the domestic ideology of the regime.
Lecture 2 slides 4-9
